books.title: The Return of the Native
books.author: Thomas Hardy
books.desc: On the wild expanse of Egdon Heath, restless Eustacia Vye dreams of escape, and the return of Clym Yeobright from Paris seems to offer her a way out.
about: Egdon Heath, a vast and ancient stretch of moorland in Wessex, is home to a small scattered community. Eustacia Vye, beautiful, proud and bored, longs for passion and a life far from the heath. Thomasin Yeobright's attempt to marry the innkeeper Damon Wildeve has gone wrong, and the faithful reddleman Diggory Venn, who loves her, watches over her. Then news comes that Thomasin's cousin Clym Yeobright, a successful diamond merchant, is returning home from Paris, and Eustacia sets her heart on him.

Hardy makes the heath itself a powerful presence, indifferent and timeless, against which his characters' desires and mistakes play out. The novel explores ambition, restlessness, family loyalty and the conflict between dreams and circumstances, with the folk customs and talk of the heath-dwellers adding humour and colour.

The Return of the Native first appeared in twelve monthly instalments in the magazine Belgravia during 1878 and was published in book form the same year. It was Hardy's sixth published novel. He had some difficulty finding a publisher for it, but reviews, though mixed, were generally positive.

books.title: Nicholas Nickleby
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.desc: Left penniless, young Nicholas Nickleby must protect his mother and sister from a scheming uncle, starting with a job at a brutal Yorkshire school.
about: When his father dies leaving the family with nothing, nineteen-year-old Nicholas Nickleby, his mother and his sister Kate turn for help to his uncle Ralph, a cold and grasping moneylender in London. Ralph sends Nicholas to work as an assistant master at Dotheboys Hall, a Yorkshire boarding school run by the cruel Wackford Squeers, where neglected boys are starved and beaten. There Nicholas befriends Smike, a broken and mistreated youth, and soon finds himself at odds with his uncle.

Dickens wanted to expose the notorious cheap Yorkshire schools where unwanted children could be left for years. Around that serious purpose he builds a lively, sprawling story full of comedy, melodrama and generosity, with characters such as the travelling theatre manager Vincent Crummles and his company.

Nicholas Nickleby was Dickens's third novel, published in twenty monthly instalments under the name Boz between March 1838 and September 1839, and in book form in 1839. The character of Squeers was inspired by a real Yorkshire schoolmaster, William Shaw.

books.title: Shirley
books.author: Charlotte Brontë
books.desc: In Yorkshire during the Luddite unrest of 1811–12, a struggling mill owner, a shy clergyman's niece and a spirited heiress face love, money and machine-breakers.
about: In the West Riding of Yorkshire in 1811 and 1812, trade is crippled by the Napoleonic Wars, and workers who fear for their jobs are breaking the new machines in the cloth mills. Robert Moore, a determined mill owner, refuses to give in to them. His quiet young cousin Caroline Helstone, who lives with her uncle the rector, loves him in secret, while the wealthy and independent heiress Shirley Keeldar, who owns the land his mill stands on, becomes Caroline's close friend.

Brontë sets a story of friendship and love against a time of social unrest, and gives a sharp account of the limited lives open to women without money or occupation. The novel contrasts its two heroines, the reserved Caroline and the bold Shirley, and mixes satire of local curates with serious reflection on work, class and independence.

Shirley was published by Smith, Elder and Co. in 1849 under the pen name Currer Bell, as Charlotte Brontë's second published novel after Jane Eyre. The attack on Robert Moore's mill draws on the real Luddite attack on Rawfolds Mill in Liversedge in 1812.

books.title: A Journal of the Plague Year
books.author: Daniel Defoe
books.desc: A London saddler records what he saw when the Great Plague of 1665 swept through the city: deserted streets, sealed houses, fear, flight and courage.
about: In 1665 bubonic plague breaks out in London. The narrator, known only by the initials H. F., is a saddler who decides to stay in the city rather than flee, and he records what he sees and hears as the epidemic grows: the weekly bills of mortality, houses shut up with their families inside, people fleeing to the country, quack doctors and prophets, mass graves, and acts of panic, cruelty and kindness.

Defoe combines lists, official regulations and statistics with vivid scenes and stories, so that the book reads at once like a historical record and a novel. It is a powerful study of how a city and its people behave in the face of a deadly epidemic, and of the choices between staying and fleeing, duty and survival.

First published in March 1722, the book appeared under the initials H. F. Defoe was only a small child in 1665, and the work is a reconstruction drawing on records and accounts of the time; it may have drawn on the memories of his uncle Henry Foe. It was published when people in England feared that an outbreak of plague in Marseilles might reach them.

books.title: The Vicar of Wakefield
books.author: Oliver Goldsmith
books.desc: A kindly, unworldly country vicar tells how his family's peaceful life is turned upside down by sudden poverty and the schemes of a charming local squire.
about: Dr Charles Primrose, a good-hearted and simple country vicar, lives contentedly with his wife Deborah and their six children until the merchant who holds his savings goes bankrupt. Forced to move to a smaller parish, the family finds itself under the eye of the young landowner Squire Thornhill, whose attentions flatter the vicar's daughters Olivia and Sophia, while a poor and eccentric gentleman, Mr Burchell, also becomes a friend of the family.

Told by the vicar himself, the story mixes gentle comedy, sentiment and moral reflection, poking fun at the family's vanities while celebrating patience, faith and kindness in misfortune. Its simple style, humour and warmth made it one of the most widely read novels of the eighteenth century.

Goldsmith wrote the novel in 1761–1762. According to a well-known story, Samuel Johnson sold the manuscript for sixty pounds in October 1762 to help his friend out of debt, but the publisher held it back until 1766, when it appeared in London.
books.author_short: Anglo-Irish novelist, playwright and poet (born 1728 or 1730, died 1774), author of The Vicar of Wakefield, She Stoops to Conquer and The Deserted Village.
author_long: Oliver Goldsmith was born in Ireland on 10 November, in 1728 according to most sources and 1730 according to others, the son of a clergyman. He studied at Trinity College Dublin, travelled in Europe, and settled in London, where he made a living as a hack writer, translator and journalist. In 1764 he became one of the first members of Samuel Johnson's literary circle, known as The Club. He died in London on 4 April 1774.

Goldsmith wrote in many forms: the novel The Vicar of Wakefield (1766), the long poem The Deserted Village (1770), and the comedy She Stoops to Conquer (1773), still performed today, as well as essays, histories and works of popular science.
